SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Psalm 90:2: "Before the mountains were born or You brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting You are God."
Revelation 4:11: "You created all things; by Your will they exist and came to be."
Exodus 3:14: "I AM WHO I AM"
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Everything we meet came from something. You have parents. A tree came from a seed. So here's a fair question, one children and philosophers both ask. If everything needs a cause, who made God?

Bertrand Russell gave it its plainest form, in a London lecture of 1927 published as Why I Am Not a Christian. At eighteen he read John Stuart Mill's Autobiography. Mill's father had taught him that the question “Who made me?” can't be answered, because it raises another: “Who made God?” Russell's conclusion: “If everything must have a cause, then God must have a cause. If there can be anything without a cause, it may just as well be the world as God.”

Richard Dawkins sharpened it in The God Delusion, in 2006: a God able to design a universe would have to be supremely complex, and so at least as improbable as the universe he's meant to explain. Then God doesn't end the chain of questions. He starts a worse one.

A good deal of this is right. Christians have sometimes argued as if everything has a cause, and stated that way, the argument refutes itself. And a designer pictured as a very complex being inside the universe, built from parts, would need explaining as much as anything he made.

Pause here and ask yourself: do the serious arguments really say everything has a cause? Or something narrower? Something narrower. In William Lane Craig's form, the kalam argument says whatever begins to exist has a cause. It says nothing about what never began. Leibniz in 1714, and Aquinas long before him, wrote about things that might not have existed. None of them says everything has a cause. Each says a certain kind of thing does.

So who made God is a fair question aimed at the wrong target. God, as Christians confess him, didn't begin, couldn't fail to be, and has no parts whose joining would need a cause. Aquinas called God altogether simple, without parts. He isn't a very large thing inside the universe, needing a maker. He's the one on whom everything else depends.

Scripture speaks of God the same way. Before the mountains were born or You brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting You are God. Nothing made him, and nothing keeps him going.

The strongest reply is Russell's parity. You've granted that something exists without a cause outside itself. Then why not the universe, or its most basic laws? It's a serious reply. Now the question isn't who made God, but which candidate can bear that weight. The universe shows marks of something that might have been otherwise. Hume suggested it might be necessary in a way we don't understand. Observation can't rule that out, or rule out God. Argument has to decide.

Then the second half: isn't proof the believer's job? Russell imagined a china teapot circling the sun, too small for any telescope. No one could disprove it, and no one would be obliged to believe it. Antony Flew argued in 1972 that the burden of proof lies on whoever affirms. He's partly right. Anyone who says God exists owes reasons. Weigh this before the answer: what does the teapot explain? Nothing. Nothing would be different without it. God is proposed to explain what everyone sees: a world that's ordered and knowable, and some things really wrong. The believer carries that burden. The unbeliever who says the universe needs no explanation carries one too.

0:19 Something rather than nothing

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Acts 17:24: "The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth"
Colossians 1:17: "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Does God actually exist? The case against is stronger than many believers admit, and nothing here forces anyone to agree. But there are reasons, each open to inspection. This film weighs one: that anything exists at all.

In 1714 Gottfried Leibniz set down what he took to be the first question we have a right to ask. “Why does something exist rather than nothing? For ‘nothing’ is simpler and easier than ‘something.’” The universe, all of space, time, matter and energy, could have been different, or not been at all.

Pause here. In 1963 the philosopher Richard Taylor asked his readers to imagine finding a large translucent ball in the woods. Would you think it simply exists, for no reason? No one would. And making the ball the size of the universe doesn't make the question go away. It makes it bigger.

This argument doesn't need the universe to have had a beginning. Thomas Aquinas held that reason alone can't show the world began in time. Alexander Pruss pictures an endless line of hens and eggs. Each hen is explained by an egg, each egg by a hen. That still leaves untouched why there's such a line rather than none. A longer chain is still a chain that needs explaining.

One. Anything that exists but might not have existed has an explanation outside itself. Two. The universe is that kind of thing. Three. So its explanation is something that exists necessarily, not made of space, time or matter.

In David Hume's Dialogues, published in 1779 after his death, one speaker objects, “why may not the material universe be the necessarily existent Being”? In 1948, debating the Jesuit Frederick Copleston on BBC radio, Bertrand Russell said, “I should say that the universe is just there, and that's all.” To him, needing a cause for the whole because each part has one is like arguing that a wall must be small because each brick is.

Much of that is true. The principle that everything has an explanation can't be proved from anything more certain than itself. In 2012 Lawrence Krauss argued that physical law can account for a universe coming to be without a creator. And if the argument said everything needs a cause, God would need one too. That question has its own film.

A fair question before the answers: if every part of the universe might not have existed, what would make the whole unable not to exist? Not every step from parts to whole is a mistake. A wall made entirely of brick is a brick wall. And the nothing in Krauss's book, the philosopher David Albert objected, is a state described by quantum laws. That's still a universe that might not have been.

The strongest reply is parity. Every account of reality stops somewhere. The atheist may stop at the universe or its basic laws, and is no more irrational for doing so. The answer is that the demand for a reason applies to what might not have been. Whether there can be a being whose existence isn't received from anything is the real crux, and philosophers divide over it. Pause and ask yourself: where do you think explanations stop, and why?

If the argument is sound, it shows a necessary being that explains the universe. That's a large part of what believers in one God mean by the word. It isn't proof in the mathematician's sense, and it isn't yet Christianity. It doesn't show that God is three persons, or that he became a man. Paul in Athens began here. The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth. Then he went straight to the resurrection, a question of history.

FULL NARRATION
If God is good, why is there so much suffering? It's the strongest reason people give for not believing, and it deserves an honest answer, not a slogan. It's old. Early in the fourth century a Christian teacher, Lactantius, preserved it to answer it, crediting it to Epicurus.

The suffering is real, and much of it looks pointless from where we stand. Some answers Christians reach for first are worse than silence. Telling a grieving mother that everything happens for a reason isn't theology. The Bible never pretends pain is good. At the grave of his friend Lazarus, Jesus wept.

Nobody can explain any one illness or disaster. When a tower fell in Siloam and eighteen people died, Jesus asked, Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you. He refused the old reading that people who suffer must be worse.

In 1955 the philosopher J. L. Mackie argued that three claims can't all be true together: God is all-powerful, God is wholly good, and evil exists. Christians answer that evil comes from misused freedom. Mackie asked why God couldn't make people who are free and always choose the good. Pause here and ask yourself. Could God make people truly free, and still guarantee that every one chooses well every time?

In 1974 Alvin Plantinga replied that a contradiction must be impossible, so a possible good reason is enough. Creatures truly free to do right and wrong may be worth the risk. Mackie later granted that evil doesn't show belief in God to be inconsistent, though he still asked whether that was a real solution. It's a real result, and a narrow one. It explains no one's suffering, and many Reformed Christians reject its view of freedom. This film doesn't choose.

In 1979 the atheist philosopher William Rowe pictured a fawn caught in a forest fire no one sees, suffering that seems to serve no good. We can see no reason for it, he said, so there probably is none. His argument hasn't been refuted. Weigh it yourself. When you can't see a reason, how sure can you be that there isn't one?

In 1984 Stephen Wykstra asked when that step is fair. See no car in your garage, and there's none. See no flea across a room, and you can't be sure. If God exists, the distance between his mind and ours is far greater. In Job, the reader is shown a reason for Job's suffering, and Job is never told it. God answers him only with questions. Rowe's reply is strong: a loving God would want to assure sufferers there is a reason, and many receive no such assurance.

Free will doesn't reach earthquakes, cancer or the suffering of animals. In 1989 Paul Draper argued that the pain in nature is what we'd expect if nothing behind it cared. Christians give several answers, and differ over them: stable laws, long ages, a creation groaning until it's set free. Each has a cost. But indifference has a cost too. It explains the pain well. It can't call it wrong, and it can't promise that it will end.

FULL NARRATION
Christians say God raised Jesus from the dead, in his body. It's fair to ask whether that happened. History can't prove a miracle. But the case is stronger than most people have been told.

In 1748 David Hume argued that the dead staying dead is as uniform as experience gets. A witness to a rising is always more likely deceived or deceiving. Bart Ehrman, an agnostic scholar, adds that the Gospels came decades later and that Rome often left the crucified unburied. Grant what's true. Legends do grow. Grief does produce visions. A claim like this should face a higher bar.

Still, nearly every historian of the period, skeptics included, accepts a short list. First, Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate. Tacitus, a Roman historian who despised Christians, recorded it. Second, his followers were soon convinced they'd seen him alive. Paul passes on a summary he received, which most scholars date within a few years. E. P. Sanders, no apologist, judged their experiences a fact. What gave rise to them, he said, he did not know.

Third, two people with every reason not to believe came to believe. Paul had been trying to destroy the church. And James was Jesus' own brother. For even His own brothers did not believe in Him. Yet James went on to lead the church in Jerusalem until he was stoned around 62. Pause here. What would it take to convince you your own brother had risen?

Fourth, the preaching began within weeks in Jerusalem, where he was buried and the claim was easiest to refute. The empty tomb itself is more disputed. Historians still divide over it. So weigh a fair question first. If you were inventing this story, who would bury Jesus, and who would find the tomb empty?

Mark names the man who buried him: Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent Council member. An inventor would more likely have picked a disciple. All four Gospels put women first at the tomb, though Josephus summed up the law as, let not the testimony of women be admitted. That was for courts, so don't press it far. The earliest opponents we know of never said the body was still there. They said it was stolen. It was an argument among first-century Jews, Jesus' followers among them, over how the tomb became empty, not whether.

Their world had words for seeing the dead. When Peter, freed from prison, knocked at a gate, the believers inside said, It must be his angel. Resurrection, N. T. Wright argues, meant something else: the bodily raising of God's people at the end of history. No one expected one man raised ahead of everyone while the world went on.

Each rival explains a part. Visions fit Peter's grief. But Paul wasn't mourning Jesus. He was hunting his followers. Legend needs time, and the list came within a few years. Fraud means men suffered for the claim while knowing where they'd put the body. And survival? David Friedrich Strauss, a skeptic, saw that a half-dead man needing bandages could never convince anyone he had conquered death.

The best reply mixes them: a lost grave, a vision, a conviction that spread, later legend. Any ordinary story, it says, beats a miracle. But the pieces multiply, each thin where it most needs to be thick. And whether a natural story beats a miracle depends on whether there's a God who might raise the dead. So ask yourself honestly. SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM

Colossians 1:17: "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together."
Genesis 1:1: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth."
Proverbs 25:2: "It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
An open Bible on one side of the table. A small telescope on the other. Plenty of people say they're enemies, and that you'll have to pick one. Pause and ask yourself where you first heard that. Then let's test it.

The war picture came from John William Draper in 1874, and Andrew Dickson White, the first president of Cornell, in 1896. They gave the modern world two forces, one marching toward the light and the other holding it back. At the center stands Galileo.

The core is true. In 1616 Rome's theologians judged the sun-centered view formally heretical. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition declared Galileo vehemently suspected of heresy. He was made to renounce his view on his knees, and he lived under house arrest until he died. The church was wrong, and Christians should say so plainly.

Galileo was a believer. He quoted Augustine: for an unbeliever to hear a Christian talk nonsense about the natural world was a disgraceful and dangerous thing. And the earth's motion hadn't been proved. Friedrich Bessel first measured its decisive sign in 1838.

When James Clerk Maxwell's Cavendish Laboratory opened at Cambridge in the 1870s, its doors carried a Psalm in Latin. Great are the works of the LORD; they are pondered by all who delight in them. Gregor Mendel, whose peas began genetics, was a friar. In 1927 Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest, argued that the universe is expanding. None of that proves Christianity. Plenty of great scientists have been unbelievers. It shows the war is a story about science, not a finding of it.

The strong objection is quieter. Science keeps explaining what God was once used to explain. In 1859 Darwin gave a natural account of how living things fit their lives. The biologist Jerry Coyne adds that science can find out it's wrong, and religion can't. A fair question before the answer comes: if every gap closes, is anything left for God?

Christians have often put God in the gaps. In 1944 Dietrich Bonhoeffer warned against it: We are to find God in what we know, not in what we don't know. Thomas Aquinas taught that God works through the causes he made, not in competition with them. An author is the cause of every line in a novel without being one of its characters. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together.

Water boils because the molecules are agitated. The kettle is on because someone wanted tea. Both answers are true, and they don't compete. If God isn't found in the gaps, Christians can't argue for him from the gaps either. The physicist Eugene Wigner, in 1960, called the power of mathematics to describe the world a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve. Science rests on something it doesn't explain.

Christians also argue over Genesis 1, and it isn't new. In the third century Origen asked how there were days before the sun. In the fourth, Basil said, For me grass is grass. Today some read six ordinary days, not long ago. Some read long ages. Some read a literary frame, God's workweek, or a cosmic temple. Some hold that God created through evolution. Each is held by believers who take Scripture seriously, and each has a hard question. This film takes no side. Which had you assumed was the only Christian view?

In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Every reading confesses that God made everything, by his word, that it was good, and that we bear his image....

FULL NARRATION
If God is real, why can't anyone see him? It's a fair question, and the Bible doesn't dodge it. Jesus said it plainly: God is Spirit. He isn't made of anything, because nothing made him.

That alone doesn't make him unreal. We know real things we can't see all the time, like love, the wind, our own thoughts. Pause here and ask yourself: how do you know the wind is there? No one has ever seen it. Everyone has seen a tree bend in it.

Christians call this general revelation: what God shows of himself to every person through the created world. The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands. But the sky can't say everything. General revelation leaves every person accountable; special revelation tells the good news.

So God spoke, to Abraham, to Moses, through the prophets, and their words were written down. At Sinai, Moses reminded Israel, “You heard the sound of the words, but saw no form; there was only a voice.”

In 1993 the philosopher J. L. Schellenberg made the argument that has shaped the debate since, in a book called Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason. Some people are open to God, yet through no fault of their own they don't believe he exists. A perfectly loving God would never leave such a person without the evidence. So there's no such God. His point isn't that God is unproved. It's that the silence itself is evidence. A loving parent doesn't hide from a child who's calling for her.

There are honest unbelievers. Many have prayed, read, asked and waited for years, and haven't come to believe. Christians have sometimes read Paul in Romans as a verdict on every doubter. Paul was describing the human race, not reading the heart of the person across the table. Scripture itself knows the ache. Isaiah says, “Truly You are a God who hides Himself.”

Blaise Pascal saw it three centuries earlier. In his Pensées, published in 1670, he wrote, “There is enough light for those who only desire to see, and enough obscurity for those who have a contrary disposition.” Weigh this: if God were as plain as the sun, could anyone still come to him freely? Michael Murray argued in 1993 that overwhelming evidence would coerce the response it meant to invite. John Hick had argued in 1966 that an obvious God would leave no room to grow freely toward him.

Schellenberg's reply is strong. Freedom, humility, growth: every one could be had inside a relationship with God, and better there. And what of a child who never resisted anything? It isn't fully answered. Christians reply in part that believing God exists is the door, not the room. A person can hold the belief and refuse the relationship.

And Christians claim God didn't stay hidden. He came near, in a way that could be missed. No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known. The Bible doesn't hide this. In Psalm 13, David asks God the same question four times. How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me? Then at Horeb, the mountain of God, a great wind tore at the rocks. Then an earthquake, then a fire. God was in none of them. And after the fire came a still, small voice. God asked Elijah a question, gave him work, and told him he wasn't alone: seven thousand were still faithful.

From Jerusalem the message went to Samaria, to Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians, and on to Rome. Worship took different shapes in different languages, but the churches confessed one faith, later written in the creeds.

The East honored Rome as first among the great churches, but held that the bishops govern together, in council. Then one Latin word, filioque, “and the Son,” added to the creed in the West: the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The West meant to guard the Son's full divinity. The East objected to the words, and to one region changing the whole church's creed. The history course says neither was simply wrong.

In 1054, at Hagia Sophia, Cardinal Humbert excommunicated the patriarch Michael Cerularius, who returned the favor. That only made visible a split already real. It was sealed in 1204, when a Western crusading army sacked Constantinople. In 1965 the pope and the patriarch lifted the old excommunications. The course finds no hero and no villain, “only two faithful traditions that loved the same Lord and lost the ability to love each other.”

The tearing was soaked in blood. Catholics killed Protestants, Protestants killed Catholics, and both killed the Anabaptists. The wars of religion ended in exhaustion, with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Nobody had won. Some divisions were over things that matter. Some were not worth what they cost. How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land? The psalm ends with a raw cry for justice. It's a prayer, not a command, and it hands that demand to God. But their center is a claim about what happened, one that could be proved false.

Some prayers argue with God. How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear? Job asks it chapter after chapter. Some psalms ask God to break the teeth of enemies. Weigh this: what would it mean for a prayer like that to be true?

For many skeptics, the deepest problem isn't that the Bible's words were changed. It's that they weren't. Laws that regulate slavery. Commands in Joshua to destroy whole towns. That moves the question from, do we have the text, to, is the God of this text good? It's a better question, and it has pages of its own.

The Bible keeps sending prophets to people who already have the Scriptures. It expects its readers to get it wrong. Paul's letters were read as Scripture very early. Yet one apostle admits another is hard to follow. Some parts of his letters are hard to understand.

What does it claim about itself? All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness. And Jesus, resting an argument on one phrase of a psalm, said the Scripture cannot be broken.

Fair objection: isn't that a circle? It's true because it says so. The first Christians couldn't have reasoned that way. They had no New Testament, only the Scriptures of Israel and the news that Jesus had been raised. They trusted Him because they believed God had raised Him. Then they received the Scriptures the way He did. He told experts in those Scriptures they'd missed what the book was for. These are the very words that testify about Me, yet you refuse to come to Me to have life.

Christians who confess the Bible as God's word differ on how to say it. Many evangelical churches confess it's without error. The Chicago Statement of 1978 says that isn't negated by “variant selections of material in parallel accounts, or the use of free citations.” Others put the conviction differently. Faithful Christians still divide over which wording is right. This film doesn't choose.

0:36 A seed, not a ghost

All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
What happens when we die is one question. This film asks how the whole story ends. Christian hope is specific: Christ's return, the dead raised in their bodies, the world judged in righteousness, and a renewed creation. The creed of Constantinople, in 381, ends right there, looking for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come.

The Bible doesn't pretend death is nothing. Jesus wept at his friend's grave. And Paul calls death an enemy. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.

So the final hope isn't a soul floating away. It's the body raised, as Jesus' body was. In 1955, at Harvard, Oscar Cullmann argued that the New Testament hopes for resurrection, not the Greek idea of an immortal soul. Critics thought he overdrew it. He still changed the conversation. Paul's picture is a seed. What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable. Pause here and ask yourself. If bodies will be raised, does what we do with bodies now matter more than we thought?

The Bible's last pages don't show people leaving the earth for the sky. They show the holy city coming down out of heaven from God. Around 180, Irenaeus argued that what passes away is the world's present form, not its substance. God doesn't say, I make new things. He says, Behold, I make all things new. Christians differ on whether this creation will be renewed or replaced, and on whether its center is the renewed earth or seeing God's face. This film doesn't choose.

Then comes judgment. To us the word sounds like condemnation. In Scripture, to judge is to set things right: to stop the oppressor and rescue the oppressed. After the wars in the former Yugoslavia, Miroslav Volf argued that only those who trust God to judge can lay down the sword of revenge. Weigh it yourself. Would a world with no final judgment be kinder, or would it tell those who suffered most that it didn't matter?

But judgment raises the hardest question. What about hell? In 1927 Bertrand Russell said, I do not myself feel that any person who is really profoundly humane can believe in everlasting punishment. The argument is about proportion. A just punishment fits the wrong. Human wrongs are finite. Endless suffering isn't. The Christian philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams asked the same in 1993. And grant what's true: the church has sometimes preached hell with relish, and used fear of it to control people.

Most of the church, with Augustine and the Reformation confessions, holds that the lost suffer conscious separation from God without end. C. S. Lewis wrote that the doors of hell are locked on the inside. Others hold conditional immortality: God alone is immortal, and the finally impenitent at last perish. Edward Fudge argued it in 1982. A smaller number, from Origen and Gregory of Nyssa to Thomas Talbott, hope God's love will restore all. Most of the church's confessions reject that hope.

Each answer carries a real difficulty. The first must face the proportion argument, and a suffering that heals no one. The second must explain why Jesus set eternal punishment beside eternal life in one sentence. The third must face his warnings, which speak of no way back. This film doesn't choose. Pause and ask yourself which difficulty seems heaviest, and why.

The strongest reply is Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov. I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don't want more suffering. The Christian answer...

The whole Bible keeps pointing back to one rescue. In Egypt, Abraham's family has become a nation of slaves, their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar. So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

From a bush that burns and isn't burned up, God sends a reluctant shepherd, Moses, to Pharaoh. Pharaoh answers with a question: who is the LORD, that I should obey him? Ten plagues reply, judgment, Exodus says, against all the gods of Egypt. The last is the death of the firstborn.

Pharaoh changes his mind and pursues with his chariots. Trapped between an army and the water, the people panic. Moses says, The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still. All night a strong east wind drives back the sea, and people who couldn't save themselves walk through on dry ground.

On the far shore Miriam leads the women with tambourines and dancing. The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation. Many scholars argue from its language that this song is among the oldest poems in the Hebrew Bible. Others date it later.

The hard question: no Egyptian text mentions Israel's slavery, the plagues, or the departure. Its most influential statement is The Bible Unearthed, by Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman, in 2001. Exodus counts about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children. That's two million or more, larger than all of Canaan then. Forty years of wandering should leave pottery, hearths, graves. Sinai has yielded nothing that fits. So, they argued, the exodus is best read as a later national epic.

Much of that is true. Nothing from Egypt or Sinai confirms the story directly, and the numbers are a real difficulty. Christians made it worse with claims like chariot wheels on the sea floor, which don't survive scrutiny.

Weigh this before the answer: would Egypt's monuments keep the memory of Egypt's humiliation? The Egyptologist James Hoffmeier argued in 1997 that Egypt's royal records rarely record defeats, and herders in tents leave little to find. What survives fits the setting: Semitic peoples in the eastern Nile Delta, a royal city named Rameses, Egyptian names like Moses and Phinehas. About 1208 BC, Pharaoh Merneptah's inscription already names Israel as a people in Canaan.

The date is argued. Counting back from First Kings 6:1 gives about 1446 BC. Others point to the name Rameses and place it in the thirteenth century. The numbers are argued too. Some take them as written. Others note that elef, the Hebrew word for thousand, can also mean a clan, which makes the company far smaller. Some think a smaller group's escape became the whole people's story. This film doesn't choose.

FULL NARRATION
The Valley of Elah runs from the hills of Judah toward the Philistine plain, a natural road for an army pushing inland. The Philistines stood on one hill and the Israelites stood on another, with the valley between them. Israel's king is Saul, chosen to fight its battles, a head taller than his men. For forty days he doesn't move.

Morning and evening a champion comes out from Gath: Goliath. The Hebrew word for champion appears only in this chapter. It means the man of the between, who steps into the space between two armies. Bronze helmet, armor of roughly 125 pounds, a spear shaft like a weaver's beam. One man for a whole people. Saul and all the Israelites were dismayed and greatly afraid.

How tall? The standard Hebrew text says six cubits and a span, about nine and a half feet. The Dead Sea Scrolls copy of Samuel and the Greek translation say four cubits and a span. Still a giant in his day. The oldest Greek manuscripts also lack whole stretches of this chapter, which suggests it circulated in more than one form.

David, the youngest of Jesse's eight sons, brings grain and bread to his brothers. Goliath shouts, the soldiers run, and David asks, Just who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God? What the soldiers hear as a threat to Israel, David hears as an insult to the living God. Pause here and ask yourself: two groups hear the same words. Why does one hear only danger, and the other hear God's name?

Saul says, you're just a boy. David answers with memory. The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine. Faith here is memory put to work in a new danger. The king's armor doesn't fit. David takes it off and chooses five smooth stones. A sling wasn't a toy. Armies had trained slingers.

The center of the chapter is a speech, not a stone. Goliath curses David by his gods. David comes in the name of the LORD of Hosts, so the whole world will know there is a God in Israel. It is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s.

David runs toward the battle line. One stone, and the champion falls facedown. Thus David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone, without a sword in his hand. Israel, frozen for forty days, charges. From here David's fame grows, and so does Saul's jealousy.

One old puzzle: in chapter 16 David already serves Saul as his harpist. Yet now Saul asks whose son he is. Some say Saul, tormented, didn't recognize him. Others note a royal marriage was promised to the winner's family, so he's asking about the father. Many scholars think two accounts sit side by side. The text doesn't settle it.

Weigh this before the answer: is this a story about believing in yourself, as if brave small people always beat big strong ones? The chapter itself says the opposite. David isn't trusting himself. He trusts the God whose name Goliath insulted. Readers still differ. Some draw from David a courage rooted in knowing whose battle it is. Others warn that First Samuel isn't a set of moral examples...

FULL NARRATION
From about 1980, Rollen Stewart held up John 3:16 signs at televised sporting events. The reference became one of the best known in the English-speaking world. But the verse belongs to a conversation.

Nicodemus was a Pharisee, most likely a member of the Sanhedrin, the council in Jerusalem. Jesus calls him Israel's teacher. He comes at night. Maybe to stay unseen. Maybe night was the hour for serious study. John means you to notice: this man comes out of the dark toward the Light.

Jesus answers with a need: no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again. The Greek word means again, or from above. Nicodemus hears a second time. Most commentators hear at least from above: a birth whose source is God. The verb is passive. Nobody gives birth to himself. Ezekiel had promised a new heart and God's own Spirit. What startled was that Israel's own teacher needed it.

One Greek word means wind, breath and spirit. The wind blows where it wishes. You hear it. You can't steer it. Pause here. What are you counting on: family, effort, standing? Jesus asked a new birth of the most religious man in the room.

Then Jesus reaches for Numbers 21. The people spoke against God and Moses. Venomous snakes came, and many died. They confessed, and the Lord told Moses, Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole. When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live. Jewish readers insisted the metal didn't heal. The Mishnah says Israel was healed when they looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven.

Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life. To a first-century ear, lifted up on a pole meant crucifixion, in public view. Yet the same word means exalted. Weigh a fair question. Why a look, and not a cure you could work for? Because faith here isn't an achievement. It's turning toward what God has provided.

For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life. Look at the small word so. It most naturally means in this way, not only so much. In 1999 Robert Gundry and Russell Howell argued that it points back to the lifting up. The word shows the love's shape: a Son given and lifted up. His love is why there is a cross.

And the world? In John it usually means humanity turned away from God, the world that did not recognize him. So the wonder isn't the world's size. It's the world's hostility. Pause here. Which is harder to believe: that God loves the world, or that he loves you in particular.

In John, to believe is to trust yourself to a person more than to agree with a statement. And eternal life is the life of the age to come, received now. Christians differ on what world and everyone imply. Arminian readers say God's saving intention reaches every person. Reformed readers, like John Owen in 1648, say God's love for the world issues in a special saving purpose...

FULL NARRATION
Psalm 23 is the best-known psalm in the Bible. Read it slowly, one picture at a time. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. In the ancient Near East, kings called themselves shepherds. Hammurabi of Babylon, in the eighteenth century BC, does it in the prologue to his laws. And God charged David to shepherd his people Israel. Psalm 23 turns that around. The king is the sheep.

The heading says, A Psalm of David. Traditional readers note that David kept sheep before he was king. Many modern scholars read the heading as marking a collection, not an author. No event is named, and it's been prayed in every generation because it isn't tied to one.

Shepherding in Judah was hard, dangerous work in dry country. Green grass and quiet water had to be found, sometimes far away. He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters. Sheep won't lie down unless they're fed and unafraid. Pause and ask yourself what you want most, and what it would take for you to rest.

He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name. Paths of righteousness can mean right paths: tracks that lead where they should, not dead ends. And notice why: for his name's sake. He's faithful to his own name.

Then the path drops into a ravine. The Hebrew word, traditionally the shadow of death, may simply mean deep darkness, where danger hides. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me. Listen to the grammar turn. Until now the psalmist has spoken about God. At the darkest point, near the center of the poem, he speaks to him. If you've come to this psalm carrying grief, notice what it doesn't promise. It doesn't promise a road around the valley. It promises company in it.

Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me. The rod was a club for driving off predators, the staff a longer stick for guiding and rescuing. Comfort here isn't softness. It's someone armed and attentive, standing between the flock and whatever hunts it.

Now the picture shifts from shepherd to host. You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. A host who took a guest into his tent was bound to protect him, even from pursuers. So this is a fugitive welcomed as an honored guest while his enemies watch, unable to act. Weigh this: the table is spread while the enemies are still there. Is that a smaller comfort, or a deeper one?

You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows. Oil on a guest's head meant welcome and honor. A cup that runs over meant lavish generosity. The guest gets more than safety.

Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life, Mercy here is chesed: loving devotion, the loyal love God has pledged to his people, love that holds when they have no claim on it. And follow can mean pursue. Enemies hunted him. Now goodness and loving devotion pursue him, all his days.

and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever. The Hebrew, as traditionally read, says I will return. The ancient Greek says dwell, spelled almost the same....

FULL NARRATION
Someone gets a hard diagnosis, or loses a person they love. And a friend, meaning well, says: everything happens for a reason. And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose. Few verses are quoted more often to people in pain, and few are quoted more carelessly.

Take the slogan seriously. It reaches for something Christians believe and call providence. God keeps the world in being. He works in and through everything that happens in it, and he directs it toward the ends he has purposed. But the slogan turns it into a code to crack, as if every loss came with a readable reason. Jesus refused that. Asked about eighteen people killed when a tower fell at Siloam, he denied they were worse sinners.

Pause here and ask yourself. Does the verse say that everything is good? Read it again before you answer. It doesn't. In our translation the subject is God. Some early manuscripts write the word God in; others don't. Either way, the sense is God's active purpose. That is both more modest and more solid than the slogan.

What does all things cover? In this chapter: present sufferings, a creation in bondage to decay, and the list in verse 35. Much of that list came from Paul's own life. He'd been beaten, shipwrecked and jailed. He never calls those things good. He says they cannot defeat God's purpose.

The verses just before are full of groaning. Creation groans. Believers groan. And the Spirit himself intercedes with groans too deep for words. Paul doesn't treat groaning as a failure of faith. The Spirit helps us in our weakness, he says, and the word for helps means taking hold of a burden together with someone. Verse 26 says what we don't know: how to pray. Verse 28 says what we do know. The promise was written from inside grief.

So what is the good? Paul leaves it open for one sentence, then defines it. To be conformed to the image of His Son. Not comfort. Not success. The good is becoming like Jesus, and nothing can defeat that purpose.

The Bible's classic picture of this is Joseph, sold by his own brothers. Years later he tells them: what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good. The same Hebrew verb, chashav, is used of the brothers and of God. One event, two intentions. The brothers are guilty of theirs. Joseph neither excuses them nor pretends the evil was good.

Here's a fair question to weigh. If God works in all things, how does that fit with real human choices? Reformed readers, from Calvin on, say God ordains all that happens, through real human causes. Arminians, from Arminius and Wesley on, say he permits much he doesn't cause. Molinists, after Luis de Molina, point to what God knows free creatures would do. They read foreknew in verse 29 differently too, yet agree its goal is likeness to Christ. And Reformed, Lutheran, Catholic and Wesleyan traditions alike deny that God is the author of sin.

And it doesn't promise that the illness will lift, or that the loss will be explained. The verse does not promise that all things are good, only that God is working in all of them. Others, the timing, grabbing a crown before God's chosen king. Many critical scholars hear sources both warm and wary toward kings. They agree on this much. The request came from a failure to trust God as king, and God took up the throne anyway.

The first king, Saul, looks the part, a head taller than anyone. But under pressure he takes things into his own hands, and Samuel tells him that obedience is better than sacrifice.

Messiah means anointed one. In Greek it's christos, Christ. Zechariah sees that king arrive: See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey. Pause and ask: what kind of king rides a donkey? A king of peace, not chariots....

Since George Mendenhall in 1954, scholars have compared Sinai and Deuteronomy with Hittite treaties: a king's history of what he'd done, then terms, witnesses, blessings and curses. They debate which parallels fit. But Israel understood its bond with God in a familiar shape: a great king's covenant with his people.

The word first appears with Noah. After the flood, God covenants with Noah and every living creature: never again a flood to destroy the earth. I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth. It rests on God's promise alone.

Abram is promised land, a family, and blessing for all the families of the earth. Years pass with no son. God takes him outside at night. “Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able. So shall your offspring be.” And Abram believed the LORD.

God seals it in an ancient form. Animals are cut in two. Whoever walked between the pieces was saying, may this happen to me if I break my word. Usually that was the weaker party. Pause here and ask yourself: who should walk that path? Abram sleeps. After dark, a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves. God alone passes through, binding himself. Many Christians see the cross here. That's a reading of the pattern, not a link the New Testament draws.

Only then the covenant, and even the commandments open with grace: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” Moses sprinkles the people and says, “This is the blood of the covenant.” Remember those words.

David wants to build God a house. Instead God promises David a house, a family line. Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever. Every later hope of a king from David's line grows here.

Start further back. Two brothers bring offerings. Cain brings some of the fruit of the soil. Abel brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock. All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Blood runs through the Bible. To many people, sacrifice looks primitive and violent, like an angry God who must be paid off. At its strongest: in 1793 Immanuel Kant argued that guilt is the most personal of all debts. Someone else can pay your money debt, but not your guilt. Pause here and ask yourself: is that what the Bible means by sacrifice?

Some of this is fair. Israel's neighbors had rites for cleansing temples and carrying evil away. And Hebrews raises the objection itself. It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. Yet Leviticus has no incantations, no demons to appease, no magic.

Why blood? The law answers in one sentence. For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar. Blood stands for life; blood poured out is a life given. And notice who's speaking. I have given it to you. Sacrifice isn't a bribe offered to a reluctant god. It's a gift God appoints, so he can live among a sinful people without consuming them.

Leviticus names five offerings. The burnt, the grain, and the peace offering, shared in a meal. The sin offering, which Jacob Milgrom called a purification offering. And the guilt offering, which came with paying back what was taken. These covered unintentional sins. For defiant sin the law gave no sacrifice, though repentance and confession opened the way to mercy.

FULL NARRATION
Here's an objection you may have heard. We don't have the original New Testament. Not one page. Only copies of copies, made by hand for centuries. So how could anyone know what it first said?

Start with what's true, because a lot of it is. The New Testament was copied by hand for nearly fifteen hundred years, until it was first printed in Greek in 1516. None of the originals survives. And the copies differ from one another in more places than there are words in the New Testament.

But think about why that number is so big. Every copyist made mistakes. So the more copies survive, the more mistakes survive with them. And no book of the ancient world survives in more copies than this one. Compare one of Rome's great histories. The first six books of the Annals of Tacitus survive in a single medieval copy. One copy has no differences to count. That doesn't make it more reliable. It makes its mistakes invisible.

So what are all those differences? Most are spelling and simple slips. A letter dropped. A word written twice. Many more you couldn't even see in English, like the order of words in a Greek sentence. Some change the meaning, but turn up in one late copy against all the rest. And a small share both change the meaning and have a real claim to be original. One leading scholar puts them at less than one percent.

Here's one of those hard cases. Jesus is speaking about the day He will return. No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. The oldest copies of Matthew have the words, nor the Son. Many later copies leave them out, most likely because they were hard to explain. And that's how we know. The older wording didn't vanish. It survived in other copies, right beside the change.

That's why the telephone game is the wrong picture. In that game, one whisper passes down one line, and nobody can check it. The New Testament was written, not whispered. And it was copied in many places at once, from Egypt to Gaul, by people who never met. A mistake made in one branch is passed down that branch and nowhere else. Lay the branches side by side, and the mistake stands out. Older copies stayed in use, too. A copy of Luke and John from about the year two hundred agrees closely with a great Bible made more than a century later. And the church argued about differences in the open. Around the year one eighty, Irenaeus said the oldest copies of Revelation read six hundred sixty-six, not six hundred sixteen. Those are people checking, not people whispering.

There are honest limits, and you should hear them. The earliest pieces we have are small, and their dates are argued over. The first stretch of copying is the part no one can see. And Christians have sometimes claimed too much. A fragment of Mark was once announced as first century. It turned out to be from the late second or early third, and the scholar who announced it apologized in public. Still, to hide in those early years, a change would have had to spread everywhere and erase the older wording in every branch. That's possible. It isn't the likeliest story.

Now set the New Testament beside the other books of its world. Homer's Iliad, the best-kept classical work, survives in about seventeen hundred and fifty manuscripts. The earliest copies of Julius Caesar's war in Gaul were made about nine hundred years after he wrote it. Historians quote those books every day, and they should. And on any honest count, the New Testament has more copies, in more languages, closer to its writing, than any of them.

All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
The Bible has been translated so many times. Hebrew to Greek, Greek to Latin, Latin to English. Like a photocopy of a photocopy. Surely the meaning is lost by now.

But that isn't how any English Bible was made. In 1526, William Tyndale translated the New Testament into English straight from the Greek. The King James translators of 1611 worked from the Hebrew and the Greek. Modern Bibles translate from editions of the Hebrew and Greek built from the manuscripts. So every translation goes back to the source. One English version's mistakes don't pass into the next. Each new translator starts again.

Still, something is always lost. The sound of a Hebrew psalm. A pun in Greek that isn't a pun in English. Scholars who love the text say so. Robert Alter, who translated the Hebrew Bible himself, warns that modern versions too often explain where they should translate. He's right that the temptation is real. Every reader should know that.

So why do English Bibles read differently? Because translators choose. Some keep close to the shape of the original, its word order and its pictures. Others aim for plain, natural speech today. Most Bibles sit somewhere between, and neither end is simply right.

Here's a place where it matters. In Romans, Paul writes a short Greek phrase that can mean faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ. Bibles differ on it, and scholars are divided. Good Bibles put the other reading in a note. But either way, the gospel of the chapter stands. Righteousness comes from God, through Christ, to all who believe. That's the pattern. The choices are fewer than the objection suggests, they're argued in the open, and the notes tell you where.

And what about verses that seem to be missing from newer Bibles? The King James was translated from the printed Greek of its day, which rested on a small number of late copies. Since then, thousands of manuscripts have been studied, many far older. In a few dozen places, they show words that copyists added over the centuries. The differences run both ways. In Matthew, the oldest copies have Jesus say that not even the Son knows the day or the hour. The King James lacks those words. Modern Bibles put them back. And the King James translators knew about variants too. In Luke, their own margin notes a verse missing from most Greek copies.

Here's something striking. The Gospels themselves are translations of a kind. Jesus spoke Aramaic, and Mark keeps some of His words. Taking her by the hand, Jesus said, “Talitha koum!” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” Mark doesn't hide the translation. He shows it to you.

The faith has always moved by translation. A scholar raised a Muslim in the Gambia, Lamin Sanneh, argued that translatability became the way Christianity spread through history. Today some part of the Bible exists in more than four thousand languages. At Pentecost, the crowd asked: How is it then that each of us hears them in his own native language?

So read more than one translation. Read the notes. Learn a little Greek or Hebrew if you can. The meaning isn't lost. You're reading through a window someone else cleaned, and you can check the glass.

apol-side-by-side.title: Does the Bible Contradict Itself? | The Gospels Read Side by Side
apol-side-by-side.description:
Can the Bible be trusted? The objection at its strongest, what the evidence shows, and what it doesn't prove.

Watch, read every word, and study further: https://www.livewellbyjamesbell.co/questions/contradictions

CHAPTERS
0:00 Side by side
0:10 Nothing new
0:30 The day He died
0:58 Two family trees
1:26 A census
1:46 Numbers
2:10 What witnesses do
2:24 Where Christians differ

FULL NARRATION
Read the Gospels side by side, and you'll find places where they don't agree. If the Bible can't keep its own story straight, why trust it?

Start here. These aren't modern discoveries. Christians noticed them from the start. Early in the third century, Julius Africanus wrote about Jesus' two family trees. Around the year 400, Augustine wrote a whole book on how the Gospels agree. The church never hid the hard places. It wrote about them.

Here's a real one. Matthew, Mark and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal. John puts Jesus' trial on the day of Preparation, when the lambs were killed. Careful scholars hold four different solutions, and each has a real weakness. The question isn't settled. But look at what all four agree on. Jesus died under Pilate, in Jerusalem, at Passover, on a Friday, and was raised on the first day of the week.

Matthew and Luke give Jesus two different lists of ancestors between David and Joseph. Some say Luke gives Mary's line. Others say one list is the royal line and the other the natural descent. Africanus offered his own answer and admitted he couldn't prove it. No solution is established. But both lists make the same claim. Jesus, through Joseph, his legal father, was of the house of David. Paul had already said so in the fifties.

Luke ties Jesus' birth to a census under Quirinius. The historian Josephus dates that census about ten years after Herod died. Several answers have been proposed, and none commands agreement. The question is open. What it touches is the date of a census, not whether Jesus was born under Herod in David's town.

In the Old Testament, Kings and Chronicles tell the same reigns and sometimes give different numbers. Forty thousand stalls in one, four thousand in the other. Many of these came from copying. Numbers were easy to miscopy, and some readings are impossible on the books' own figures. And they show something else. The writer of Chronicles had the older books open in front of him, and he didn't hide them.

Here's the pattern. Independent accounts that agree at the center and differ at the edges are what historians usually find when a real event has been told more than once. Differences at the edges don't turn the center into legend.

Christians also differ on how to say what this means. Some hold that Scripture is without error in all that it affirms. Others hold it is infallible in what God gave it to teach, without requiring every number or date to be harmonized. Both confess that God has spoken in Scripture, and that it is the church's final authority.

So read slowly. Put the accounts side by side. Notice the hard places. You'll find that nearly every one sits at the edge of a story whose center they share.

apol-what-the-ground-says.title: Does Archaeology Confirm the Bible? | What the Ground Says
apol-what-the-ground-says.description:
Can the Bible be trusted? The objection at its strongest, what the evidence shows, and what it doesn't prove.

Watch, read every word, and study further: https://www.livewellbyjamesbell.co/questions/old-testament/what-archaeology-shows

CHAPTERS
0:00 What the ground says
0:18 What didn't hold up
0:39 The house of David
1:02 A rebel king
1:25 A bird in a cage
1:48 Pick against pick
2:03 Independent witnesses
2:17 What the ground can't do

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
2 Kings 3:5: "But after the death of Ahab, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Does archaeology prove the Bible? Some say every dig confirms it. Others say the spade has come up empty. No trace of the exodus, a Jericho without walls, little sign of Solomon's great kingdom. The honest answer is neither.

Start with what didn't hold up. For years, a shaft in Jerusalem was linked to the way David's men took the city. Later digging suggests it wasn't reachable in David's time. Gates once credited to Solomon are now dated by some archaeologists to the century after him. And for the exodus and the conquest, the ground is mostly silent.

But from the ninth century before Christ, Israel's neighbors and enemies start writing things down. In 1993, at Tel Dan, diggers found pieces of an Aramaic victory stone. A king of Aram boasts of killing a king of the house of David. Most scholars take it as the earliest known mention of David's dynasty by name, more than a century after him.

In 1868, in Moab, a black stone was found. King Mesha records how Omri, king of Israel, had oppressed his land, and how he broke free. Second Kings tells it from Israel's side. But after the death of Ahab, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel. The two accounts don't fit together in every detail. They agree on the main fact.

Then Assyria. Sennacherib invaded Judah, and the Bible says Hezekiah paid him thirty talents of gold. Sennacherib's own annals boast that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage. They give the same thirty talents of gold. The silver differs. And notice what the annals never claim. They never say the city was taken.

Hezekiah also cut a tunnel to bring water into the city. It still runs under Jerusalem. An inscription found inside it in 1880 tells how the diggers, working toward each other, struck pick against pick, and the water flowed.

That's what independent sources look like. They agree on the main facts, differ in the details, and each tells the story from its own side. Where the writers of Kings can be checked, they behave like historians of a kind.

But a stone can't show that God spoke to Moses. Inscriptions confirm names and events, not meanings. And silence cuts both ways. It can't prove a great kingdom under Solomon, and it can't prove a small one. Claims of proof and claims of disproof both say more than archaeology can.

The faith doesn't rest on a spade. It rests on what God did in history, above all the resurrection. Archaeology shows the Old Testament's world was real. It was never going to be the ground of faith, and it hasn't taken it away.

apol-who-chose-the-books.description:
Can the Bible be trusted? The objection at its strongest, what the evidence shows, and what it doesn't prove.

Watch, read every word, and study further: https://www.livewellbyjamesbell.co/questions/authors/did-constantine-decide-the-bible

CHAPTERS
0:00 Who chose the books?
0:15 What Nicaea did
0:40 The emperor's own bishop
1:08 Before any emperor
1:31 The other gospels
1:53 How the church judged
2:22 What the objection gets right
3:00 Which faith came first

FULL NARRATION
You've probably heard this one. The emperor Constantine decided what went into the Bible, at the Council of Nicaea in 325. He kept the books that suited the church in power, and buried the rest.

So what did Nicaea actually do? The bishops answered Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being, and they wrote a creed against him. They dealt with the date of Easter, a split in the church in Egypt, and twenty rules of church order. Not one of their surviving decisions lists the books of Scripture. Constantine did order fifty copies of the Scriptures for his new city. His letter names no books.

Here's the telling part. Eusebius, a bishop who was at Nicaea and admired Constantine, wrote a list of the New Testament books in those very years. The four Gospels, Acts and Paul's letters were accepted everywhere. A few, like James, Jude and Second Peter, were still disputed. And he wasn't sure where to put Revelation. If the emperor had settled it, his admirer had every reason to say so. He doesn't.

Go back further. In the 150s, Justin Martyr describes Christians on Sunday reading the memoirs of the apostles, which, he says, are called Gospels. Around 180, Irenaeus says the Gospels can't be more or fewer than four. That's a century and a half before Nicaea, while Christians were still a persecuted minority.

But weren't there other gospels? There were. Thomas, Peter, Mary, Judas. Most scholars date them to the second century, after the four. None is earlier than the four on the usual dating, though some argue parts of Thomas carry older sayings. Thomas is a collection of a hundred and fourteen sayings. It says nothing of Jesus' death and resurrection.

Around the year two hundred, a bishop named Serapion found a church reading a gospel under Peter's name. At first he let them read it. Then he read it himself, found much in it sound and some things added, and judged it against what his churches had received. That isn't a council imposing a list. It's a pastor reading a book and testing it. One historian who studied all of this concluded, in effect, that no one chose the four Gospels. They were received.

The objection does get some things right. Early Christianity was varied. Paul himself wrote against people preaching another gospel. The church did test books by their teaching, as well as by their link to the apostles and their use across the churches. And the edges took centuries to settle. The first list that matches our twenty-seven books exactly comes from Athanasius, in 367. He was driven out of his city five times. He was no emperor's man. Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Bibles still differ in the Old Testament. But all of them share the same twenty-seven books of the New.

So the real question is which faith was there first. The earliest Christian writings we have, Paul's letters from the fifties, already carry the faith of the four Gospels. Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day. None of the gospels the church set aside is attested that early.

No emperor made the Bible. The churches received it, argued over its edges in the open, and said why. You can read their reasons. Then read the books.

apol-written-too-late.description:
Can the Bible be trusted? The objection at its strongest, what the evidence shows, and what it doesn't prove.

Watch, read every word, and study further: https://www.livewellbyjamesbell.co/questions/authors/written-decades-later

CHAPTERS
0:00 Written too late?
0:13 What's true in it
0:39 Inside one lifetime
0:49 Earlier than any Gospel
1:25 How historians treat gaps
1:44 Anonymous, or unknown?
2:30 The earliest witnesses
2:49 The strongest reply
3:11 What stays open

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
1 Corinthians 15:3-4: "For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,"
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Here's another objection. The Gospels were written decades after Jesus, by people who never met Him, under names someone added later. If that's true, why trust what they say?

Again, start with what's true. Jesus was crucified around the year thirty. Most scholars date Mark around seventy, Matthew and Luke later, and John in the nineties. That's forty to sixty-five years. Some able scholars argue for earlier dates, but that's a minority view, and it has to be argued, not assumed. And none of the four Gospels names its author in its own text.

But think about what a gap like that is. It sits inside a single lifetime. People who had known Jesus were still alive. Many more had known them.

And we have writing from inside the gap. Paul's letters, from the fifties. In one of them, Paul passes on a summary he says he himself received. For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, Most scholars, including many with no stake in Christianity, think that summary took shape within a few years of the cross. And Paul says he stayed fifteen days with Peter in Jerusalem, and later met James and John.

Historians of the ancient world work with far bigger gaps than this. One of our main accounts of Alexander the Great's campaigns, by Arrian, was written more than four centuries after them. Historians still use it, carefully. So the question isn't only how long the gap was. It's what stood inside it.

Now the names. It's true the titles, According to Matthew and the rest, were almost certainly added by others. But anonymous isn't the same as unknown. Every early copy that keeps a title gives the same four names. No early copy gives another. If churches across the Roman world had guessed, you'd expect a Gospel of Andrew in one place and of Philip in another. We find none. And look at two of the names. Mark and Luke weren't among the Twelve. Mark is remembered as the man who turned back partway through Paul's first mission. When people did write gospels under famous names, they chose apostles, like Peter. Mark and Luke look less like a grab for authority than a memory nobody was free to improve.

Early in the second century, a writer named Papias passed on what an older teacher told him: that Mark had been Peter's interpreter, and wrote down what Peter remembered. And Luke never claims to have seen Jesus. He says he carefully investigated what the eyewitnesses handed down. That's just what the church always said of him.

A skeptic can answer that witnesses alive somewhere don't help unless the writers used them. And memory is fragile. That's fair. Memory bends, and a witness interprets as well as remembers. But this story was told in churches where Peter, James and John had preached, among people who had heard them. It wasn't free to drift wherever anyone wished.

Some things stay open. Whether the apostle Matthew wrote the Gospel that bears his name, or stands behind it. Who the beloved disciple was. Exactly when Mark wrote. Faithful Christians differ on those, and honest scholars live with them.

What the church confesses doesn't hang on a decade. It hangs on whether these books tell the truth about a man crucified under Pontius Pilate and raised on the third day. And the earliest witness to that claim is older than any of the four.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The Word became flesh
0:12 What the church confesses
0:35 A God who dwells
0:54 The promised king
1:10 The Word became flesh
1:32 Truly human, truly God
1:54 Guarding both sides
2:28 Where Christians differ
2:57 What it changes

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
John 1:14: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth."
Hebrews 4:15: "For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Christians say God became a man. So which was Jesus? God only wearing a body? Or a good man later called God? The church's answer is neither.

It's called the incarnation, from the Latin word for flesh. The eternal Son of God, without ceasing to be God, became a man, Jesus of Nazareth, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. He took a whole human nature, body and soul, mind and will. One person, fully God and fully man.

The Old Testament doesn't say this outright. But it builds a longing. At Sinai, Israel heard a voice but saw no form. Yet God had His people build a tent so He could dwell among them. And His glory filled it. Later, Solomon dedicated the temple and asked if God would really dwell on earth.

The promises of a coming king lean the same way. Isaiah spoke of a son called Immanuel, God with us. Two chapters later, a child from David's house is called Mighty God. And Malachi said the Lord would suddenly come to His temple.

Then John says it plainly. The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. In Greek, made His dwelling means pitched His tent, the same word used for the tabernacle. The glory that filled that tent is now seen in a man.

The Gospels show a real human life. He grows, and He gets hungry. He sleeps in a boat. He weeps at a friend's tomb. In Gethsemane He's deeply troubled, and yields His will to the Father's. Yet He forgives sins, which only God can do. He commands the sea, and it obeys. No wonder the disciples asked who this could be.

The early church guarded both sides. Around the year 110, Ignatius of Antioch answered those who said Christ only seemed to have a body. He was truly born, Ignatius wrote, and truly suffered and died. When a teacher denied Christ a human mind, Gregory of Nazianzus answered that what Christ did not take on, He did not heal. In 451, the Council of Chalcedon set the boundaries. One person in two natures, neither mixed nor changed, neither divided nor separated.

Christians who confess all this still differ on some questions. Would the Son have come if we had never sinned? Thomas Aquinas judged it more fitting to say no, since Scripture gives the remedy for sin as the reason. John Duns Scotus said yes, because Christ was the goal of creation from the start. And when Paul says Christ emptied Himself, did He veil His glory, or lay aside the use of some divine powers for a time? Christians answer both ways.

When Christians ask what God is like, they look at Jesus. He spent most of His years in a small town, working with His hands. Nothing human is beneath God's notice. And the One Christians pray to has been where they are. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin. He still bears a human nature in heaven. The hope isn't escape from being human, but renewal, soul and body.

He was rich and became poor for others, and Paul makes that the pattern for how Christians treat each other. God isn't a distant idea. He has a face and a name, and pitched His tent among us.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Right with God
0:11 A word from the courtroom
0:29 Counted as righteous
0:52 Freely, by grace
1:17 Paul and James
1:36 How the church read it
1:56 Where Christians differ
2:53 What they share
3:14 For an ordinary day

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Genesis 15:6: "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness."
Romans 8:1: "Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
It's the oldest question in religion. How can a person be in the right with God? Job asked it. So has anyone who felt they didn't measure up.

The Bible answers with a word from the courtroom. Justify. To justify is what a judge does when he rules that someone stands in the right. But God will not acquit the guilty. And the Psalms admit no one alive is righteous before Him. So how can a just judge rule for the guilty?

The first hint of an answer comes under a night sky. God shows Abram the stars and promises children beyond counting. Abram is old and childless. Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness. That's centuries before the law. Paul reads it as God counting a man righteous whose only part was trust in a promise.

Jesus told of a tax collector who only asked for mercy. He went home justified, and the Pharisee did not. Paul says sinners are justified freely, by God's grace, through what Christ has done. The cross is how God stays just while putting the ungodly in the right. Their sin is dealt with, not waved away. The gift is received through faith, not earned by keeping the law.

But James writes that a person is justified by deeds, and not by faith alone. Most interpreters say Paul asks how a sinner is accepted, while James attacks a faith that does nothing. Others think James means the final verdict. Either way, the faith that receives the gift is never alone.

The earliest Christian writers repeated Paul's words without a quarrel. Augustine taught that justification is wholly God's gracious act, and took the Latin word to mean making righteous. With Martin Luther, the Reformation made it a dividing question. The Catholic Church answered at the Council of Trent, in 1547.

Christians differ here. Lutheran and Reformed Christians teach that justification is a verdict. God forgives the sinner and credits to him Christ's righteousness. Faith is the empty hand that receives it. A changed life always follows, but it's never the ground of the verdict. Catholics teach that God doesn't only forgive. He truly makes the sinner righteous, pouring His love into the heart by the Holy Spirit. Grace comes first, and no one can earn it. Faith is the root, joined with hope and love. Because it's a real change, it can grow, be lost through grave sin, and be restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance. The Orthodox confess salvation as entirely God's gift in Christ, but their main picture is theosis, union with God, not a courtroom. They generally see the Western quarrel as resting on a line between declaring and making righteous that they never drew.

All of them reject the idea of standing before God on your own record, apart from grace. In 1999, the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed a joint declaration of shared basic truths, leaving real differences open. Many confessional Lutherans, Reformed and evangelicals judged it papered over them.

Someone who keeps their own accounts with God is never at rest. The books never balance. Being justified brings peace with God. Someone who knows they're accepted can afford to tell the truth about their sin. The tax collector and the Pharisee, the churchgoer and the latecomer, stand on the same footing. The acquitted have every reason to pass that mercy on.

Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. No one can put themselves in the right with God. It's His work, and it comes as a gift.
