0:00 In Christ
0:11 What the church confesses
0:28 A small phrase
0:44 The roots
1:08 The true vine
1:36 Died and raised with him
2:04 Through the centuries
2:28 Where Christians differ
3:10 What it changes

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
John 15:5: "I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing."
Colossians 3:3: "For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Read the New Testament and you keep running into a small phrase. In Christ. What does that mean? How can one person be in another?

A Christian isn't only helped by Jesus from a distance. A Christian is joined to him. What's true of him becomes true of them. They died with him, were raised with him, and will appear with him. The Holy Spirit makes that bond, and faith receives it.

Paul uses it, and close cousins like in him, all through his letters. In 1892 the scholar Adolf Deissmann counted a hundred and sixty-four of them. He also reaches for words that mean with. Crucified with. Buried with. Raised with.

The Old Testament never says this outright. It gives the ground the idea grows from. A God who makes his home in the middle of his people. A Hebrew word for clinging, used when husband and wife become one flesh. The prophets made that bond a picture of God's love. And one standing for many, the way Adam's choice reached the whole human race.

Israel had been God's vine. Jesus took the picture for himself. I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing. Belonging to God's people now means being a branch in him. Later the risen Jesus asked Saul, who was persecuting the church, why Saul was persecuting him. To strike the church is to strike Christ.

For Paul, Adam and Christ each stand for a whole humanity. Joined to Adam, people share his death. Joined to Christ, they share his life. Believers were buried with him through baptism, so they could walk in a new life. Every spiritual blessing is given in him. Chosen in him. Redeemed in him. Sealed with the Spirit in him. And no one is joined to him alone. Together, believers are his body.

Around the year 180, Irenaeus taught that Jesus went back over the ground where Adam failed, obeying where Adam disobeyed, so those joined to him share his victory. In his Institutes, John Calvin wrote that as long as Christ stays outside us, all he suffered and did is no use to us. The Holy Spirit, he said, is the bond that joins us to him.

Christians describe this union in different ways. Reformed Christians say believers receive two gifts in him, never separated. Declared right with God, and made new. Lutherans say Christ comes through Word and sacrament. Luther pictured a joyful exchange. Christ takes the believer's sins and gives his righteousness. Roman Catholics say baptism joins a person to Christ and his body, the church, and the Eucharist feeds that union. The Orthodox call it theosis, sharing by grace in God's life, while God's essence stays beyond every creature. Every one of them insists it's by grace. A creature joined to God is still a creature.

This changes where a Christian finds who they are. For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God. Failure and success are real. But they don't define someone whose life is found in another. Suffering isn't proof that God is absent. It can be one of the ways the union is lived. And the people beside them at the Lord's Supper, however different, belong to the same body.

Even death doesn't break it. Paul calls believers who have died the dead in Christ, still in him, waiting for the resurrection. No part of a Christian's life, not even its end, is outside of Christ.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Growing in grace
0:12 What holy means
0:36 Two tenses
1:00 Holy to the Lord
1:22 Set apart in Christ
1:45 Who does the work?
2:10 Through the centuries
2:25 Where Christians differ
3:08 In ordinary life

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Philippians 2:13: "For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose."
1 Thessalonians 5:24: "The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
You've trusted Christ, and you know you're forgiven. So why are you still fighting the same old sins? And if God already accepts you, does it matter how you live?

The Bible answers both with one word. Sanctification. To be holy is first to belong to God, set apart for him, and then to become like him. Sanctification is the Holy Spirit's lifelong work of setting believers apart and making them like Jesus Christ. It isn't justification, God's verdict that you're in the right, but the two never come apart.

Scripture speaks in two tenses. Believers already are sanctified, and they're being sanctified. Paul wrote to a church full of factions and lawsuits, and still told them they'd been sanctified. A saint, in the Bible, isn't a rare hero. It's any member of God's people. One tense is still to come. When Christ appears, his people will be like him.

Holiness starts as God's claim. At Sinai he claims a whole people, holy because he chose them. Leviticus calls Israel to be holy as God is holy, then to leave the edges of the harvest for the poor. Holiness meant being like a God who cares for the poor. Through Ezekiel, God promised his people a new heart, and his Spirit within them.

The night before he died, Jesus prayed for his disciples to be sanctified, and set himself apart for their sake. Hebrews says believers were sanctified once for all by his sacrifice, and are still being sanctified. Is grace a license to sin? No, says Paul, because believers have died with Christ and been set free from sin.

So who does the work, God or you? Paul says both. Continue to work out your salvation, he writes. Then he says why. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose. And the Spirit grows one fruit, not many. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.

In the late fourth century, Gregory of Nyssa called perfection endless growth into God, because God has no end. Augustine taught that holiness itself is a gift of grace, and that no one in this life is without sin.

Christians differ on how far holiness reaches in this life. Reformed churches teach a decisive break with sin's rule, then slow growth, never finished in this life. Lutherans stress living from forgiveness, a daily return to baptism, and not trusting your own progress. Wesleyan and Holiness churches teach entire sanctification, a heart so full of love that the will is wholly God's, though not sinless perfection. Keswick teaching calls for a decisive act of surrender and faith, then a life of consistent victory. Catholics speak of grace growing through the sacraments, the Orthodox of theosis, lifelong growth into likeness to God.

So because you're already set apart and loved, failure doesn't undo your standing. And because God means to make you like Christ, you can't make peace with your sin either. The means are ordinary: Scripture, prayer, confession, the Lord's Supper, other believers, small duties, even hardship. Growth is often slow, and others tend to see it before you do. Zechariah saw a day when every cooking pot in Jerusalem would be holy. Holiness reaches into how you pay a worker, treat the disabled, talk about people and forgive.

It all rests on a promise. The God who began the work will finish it. The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it. Christians press on, not to earn the day Christ appears, but because it's coming.

CHAPTERS
0:00 He will come again
0:13 What the church confesses
0:46 What the prophets hoped for
1:09 What Jesus said
1:34 The first Christians
1:54 Confessed, never calculated
2:21 Where Christians differ
3:05 What it changes

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Acts 1:11: "“Men of Galilee,” they said, “why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.”"
Revelation 22:20: "He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!"
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Do Christians really believe Jesus is coming back? And if they do, why can't they agree on how? Both are fair questions. Start with what every ancient creed confesses.

The same Jesus who was crucified, raised and taken up into heaven will come again. In person, in His body, in public glory. He'll raise the dead, judge the world, and bring God's kingdom to completion in a renewed creation. As He was taken up, two men dressed in white said it plainly. “Men of Galilee,” they said, “why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.”

The Old Testament doesn't speak of a second coming, because it hasn't seen the first. It hopes that God Himself will come. In a vision, Daniel sees one like a Son of Man coming with the clouds, who is given a kingdom that will never be destroyed. The prophets saw one great Day of the Lord. The New Testament finds it in two acts, and the first brought mostly mercy.

Jesus spoke of His return most often with the title Son of Man, from that vision. His coming, He said, would be as public as lightning, as sudden as the flood, and as unexpected as a thief. But the time is hidden, even from the angels in heaven. Only the Father knows it. So His stories about it all teach one thing. Keep watch by being faithful at the work you were given.

Paul wrote to Christians grieving their dead. When the Lord comes, he told them, the dead in Christ will rise first. The earliest believers prayed for that day in Aramaic, marana tha, which means Our Lord, come. Every time the church shares the bread and cup, it proclaims His death until He comes.

In 381, the creed received at Constantinople said He will come again in glory, and His kingdom will have no end. But the creeds never set a date. In the nineteenth century, William Miller calculated that Christ would return in 1843 or 1844. When October 22, 1844 passed, it became known as the Great Disappointment. Every calculation so far has failed.

Christians do divide over the order of events, most of all over the thousand years in Revelation 20. Amillennialists read the thousand years as this present age, with Christ reigning now from heaven. Postmillennialists expect the gospel, by the Spirit's power, to bring the nations broadly under Christ's rule before He returns. Historic premillennialists expect Christ to return before a thousand-year reign on earth, with the church passing through the final tribulation. Dispensational premillennialists expect God's promises to Israel to be kept to the letter, and Christ to come for His church in a rapture, most say before a seven-year tribulation. Each view argues from Scripture, and all of them confess the same return.

So what does it change? It means the story has an ending, and the ending has a face. It changes grief. Paul doesn't tell believers not to grieve, only not to grieve like those without hope. It gives ordinary work weight. Waiting for Him doesn't mean staring at the sky, but caring for the people and the work entrusted to you. The hidden day keeps you steady, because the outcome is secure, and alert, because no one knows the hour.

The Bible ends with His promise and the church's answer. He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! Until then, keep watch, keep working, and keep praying it.

CHAPTERS
0:00 In the beginning
0:12 What the church confesses
0:30 The first sentence
0:51 And it was good
1:05 Through the Son
1:27 Out of nothing
1:53 Where Christians differ
2:57 What it changes

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Genesis 1:1: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth."
Revelation 21:5: "And the One seated on the throne said, “Behold, I make all things new.” Then He said, “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.”"
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Where did all this come from? The stars, the sea, the breath in your lungs. And if God made it, why do Christians argue over the Bible's first page?

The church confesses that God made everything other than Himself. He made it freely, by His word, from nothing, and it was good. The world isn't God, and it isn't an accident. It's a gift from a God who needed nothing, and He holds it in being every moment.

The Bible's first sentence is a confession. In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Other nations told it differently. In the Babylonian epic, the Enuma Elish, the world is built after a war among the gods. Genesis has one God, no battle, and no rival. He speaks, and things come to be.

Even the sun and moon, which Israel's neighbors worshiped as gods, are simply lights, set in the sky to mark the seasons. Seven times God sees that what He made is good. The last time, it's very good.

The New Testament says what Genesis couldn't yet say. God made the world through His Son. Colossians says everything was made in Him, through Him, and for Him, and in Him it all holds together. The Spirit hovered over the waters too. Creation is the work of one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The first Christians taught in a world shaped by Greek thinkers. Plato pictured a divine craftsman shaping material already there, and Aristotle held the world had always existed. Around the year 180, Theophilus of Antioch answered that God made all things out of nothing. The creeds made it the whole church's confession. One God, maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible.

Christians differ most over how to read the six days, and the age of the earth. Young-earth creationists read the days as ordinary days and the genealogies as a real, fairly short chronology, so the earth is thousands of years old. Scripture's plain sense, they say, should govern how the evidence is read. Old-earth creationists say the earth is billions of years old, and the Hebrew word for day can mean a long period. Across those ages God acted directly, bringing new kinds of life into being. The framework view sees the days arranged by topic, not by clock, three days forming realms and three filling them. So the chapter teaches who made the world, not how old it is. Evolutionary creationists believe God created life through the long process of evolution, which He sustains and directs. A patient process, they say, is no less God's act than an instant one. Each view argues from Scripture. They differ on how to read the days, not on who made the world.

So what does it change? Breath, food, work, beauty and your own body all come as gifts. Because creation is good, you're free to enjoy it without guilt, and bound to care for it. Because it isn't God, you're free to study it, farm it, and build with it without fear. Isaiah told exiles who felt forgotten to look up. The One who made the stars calls each one by name, and He doesn't grow weary.

Creation groans now, Paul says, waiting to be set free from decay. But the Bible begins and ends with God making. And the One seated on the throne said, “Behold, I make all things new.” Then He said, “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.” His last verdict over His world will be the same as His first. Good.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Holy, loving, just
0:13 What the church confesses
0:39 In His own words
1:07 Mercy and justice
1:30 Echoed through Israel
1:51 Seen in a life
2:22 An old mistake
2:41 Where Christians differ
3:26 What it changes

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Exodus 34:6-7: "The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished"
Revelation 4:8: "Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!"
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
What is God like? Many have a quick answer. The God of the Old Testament is angry. The God of Jesus is kind. But the Old Testament itself says otherwise.

Christians speak of God's attributes, the Bible's ways of saying what God is like. He is holy, righteous, faithful, merciful, patient, and wise. All-powerful, all-knowing, present everywhere, eternal, and unchanging. They never pull against each other. His justice is always loving, and His love is always just and holy.

Israel had just worshiped the golden calf when Moses asked to see God's glory. Then the LORD passed in front of Moses and called out. The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished

Notice who heard it. A people who had just broken the covenant. Mercy and justice stand together, but not evenly. Loving devotion to a thousand generations, judgment to the third and fourth. Loving devotion translates the Hebrew word chesed. It's loyal, committed love, most often within a covenant. No single English word catches it.

No description of God is echoed more in the Old Testament. Moses, Nehemiah, the psalmists, and Joel prayed it back to Him. Jonah even complained that God was exactly this merciful to Nineveh. Isaiah heard the seraphim calling out, holy, holy, holy. In Hosea, that holiness shows itself as mercy.

John says the Word made flesh was full of grace and truth, and many hear an echo of loving devotion and faithfulness. In Jesus, God's character is seen. His compassion on the crowds, His anger at the temple, His faithfulness to the cross. At the cross, Paul says, God is both just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus. Justice and mercy meet there. John puts it in three words. God is love, a love defined by His sending His Son.

That quick answer is old. In the second century, Marcion divided a just Creator from a loving Father. Around the year 180, Irenaeus answered that the one God is both good and just. The words to Moses are full of mercy, and Revelation is full of judgment. It's one character.

Christians differ here. How does God's steady character fit His real response to human choices? In one chapter, the LORD regrets making Saul king, and Samuel says the Glory of Israel does not change His mind. Classical theists, like Thomas Aquinas, say God is unchanging in His being, timeless, and not overcome by passions. Regret, they say, is true speech fitted to human understanding. Others, like Nicholas Wolterstorff, see God's eternity as endless time, because the Bible's God speaks, waits, and hears prayer. Still others, like Jürgen Moltmann, say God truly suffers, from love freely chosen. They point above all to the cross.

Believe God is powerful but not quite good, and you'll obey out of fear. Believe He's good but not quite able, and you'll pray without hope. Scripture holds them together. His power is always the power of His goodness. In grief, His faithfulness is the reason to keep speaking to Him. In guilt, His mercy is the reason to return. In confusion, His wisdom is the reason to wait.

At the Bible's end, the four living creatures take up Isaiah's cry. Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come! The God who is faithful and cannot lie will keep what He has promised.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Born again
0:11 What Christians confess
0:24 Trouble in the heart
0:42 A new heart
1:00 By night
1:21 A new creation
1:35 Through the centuries
1:53 Where Christians differ
2:56 In ordinary life

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
John 3:3: "Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.”"
John 3:8: "The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.”"
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Can a person really change? Not just try harder, but change at the root? Christians answer with two familiar words. Born again.

Theologians call it regeneration, God's act of giving spiritual life to people who can't give it to themselves. It's the Holy Spirit's work inside a person, and it shows in a changed life.

The Old Testament finds the trouble in the heart, which in Hebrew is the center of thought, will and desire. Before the flood, the Lord sees that every inclination of the human heart is evil. After it, he says so again. The flood cleansed the earth, but not the heart.

Through Ezekiel, a priest among the exiles in Babylon, God commands his people to make themselves a new heart. Then he promises to give them one, a heart of flesh for a heart of stone. Next, Ezekiel sees a valley of dry bones. Breath enters them, and they live.

Nicodemus, a Pharisee on the ruling council, comes to Jesus by night. Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.” The Greek word can mean again, or from above. Nicodemus hears the first. Many interpreters think both are meant.

Paul calls anyone in Christ a new creation. He also writes that God saved us through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. And Peter writes that believers are born again through the living and enduring word of God.

The early church tied the new birth closely to baptism. Around the year 155, Justin Martyr wrote that believers were brought to water and regenerated. In the eighteenth century, revivals made the new birth their banner, in the preaching of George Whitefield and John Wesley.

Christians differ on two questions. First, the order of faith and new birth. Reformed Christians teach that people dead in sin can't believe until God makes them alive. So the new birth comes first, in logic if not in time. Wesleyan and Arminian Christians teach that no one turns to God by their own power, but grace goes before, so a person can believe or refuse. When they believe, God gives the new birth. Second, baptism. Jesus spoke of being born of water and the Spirit. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran churches, and many Anglicans, teach that God gives the new birth through baptism, to infants as well as adults, a gift to be lived in faith and repentance. Baptists and other believers' churches teach that the Spirit gives new birth through the word when a person believes, and baptism is its public sign, for those who profess faith. All of them confess the new birth as God's work by his Spirit, not a fresh start you make yourself.

That's humbling. Nicodemus was a respected teacher, and still had to be born again. It's hopeful, too. No one is too far gone. Ezekiel's dry bones lived by the breath God sent. People come to faith in many ways, some suddenly, some so gradually they can't name the day. What matters is the signs of life now. Trust in Christ, love for other believers, a desire to do right, a readiness to confess sin. Those signs are often weak. A newborn is still newly born.

The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.” The new birth starts a life that will grow, the first taste of the renewal God has promised the whole creation.

A clear film on what Christians believe, read straight from the Bible. Where faithful Christians differ, the film names the views and takes no side.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Turning around
0:14 A change of direction
0:34 A God who seeks
1:01 A son comes home
1:26 Remorse or repentance
1:45 No sin too great
2:19 Where Christians differ
3:12 For an ordinary day

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Luke 15:20: "So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him."
1 John 1:9: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
What do you do with something you wish you'd never done? You can hide it, excuse it, or despair over it. Or you can turn around. The Bible calls that repentance.

Repentance is turning back to God. It includes sorrow for sin, but it's more than regret. It's a change of mind that becomes a change of direction, away from sin and toward the God who offers mercy. Forgiveness is God's side of the turning. He releases the guilty from the debt of their sin, freely.

When the first man and woman hide among the trees, the LORD God calls out, Where are you? King David commits adultery and murder. Confronted by the prophet Nathan, he says, I have sinned against the LORD. Nathan answers, The LORD has taken away your sin. The consequences in David's house remain, but the sin is gone. Isaiah urges the wicked to return to the LORD, for He will freely pardon.

Jesus said He came to call sinners to repentance. In His story of a lost son, the young man comes to his senses and heads home, a confession ready. So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him. The father doesn't wait for the speech to be finished.

The Gospels set two failures side by side. Judas, filled with remorse, gave back the silver. Peter had denied Jesus three times. Jesus restored him with three questions and a commission. The difference wasn't the size of the sin. It was where each man turned.

In 250, during the Decian persecution, many Christians sacrificed to the gods. Cyprian of Carthage supported taking them back after penance. Novatian, at Rome, refused. The church's mainstream held that no sin is beyond forgiveness for the one who repents. Jesus warned that whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven. That has generally been understood as a settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit's witness to Christ, not a single failure a troubled believer fears he has committed.

Christians differ on how repentance fits with faith, and on confession. Reformed Christians teach that repentance is God's gift to a new heart, rising with faith and lasting for life. Lutherans teach that the law exposes sin and troubles the conscience, the gospel creates faith, and repentance is a daily return to baptism. Wesleyans teach that grace awakens a sinner to repent, ordinarily before justifying faith, and that believers keep repenting of sin that remains. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that Christ gave His apostles authority to forgive sins, and that sins after baptism are forgiven through a sacrament. In Catholic teaching, a priest pronounces absolution in Christ's name. The Orthodox speak of confession above all as healing. Lutherans keep private confession and absolution too, as a gift.

Repentance isn't punishing yourself. You don't have to feel sorry enough before God will listen. It's concrete. Zacchaeus paid people back. Those forgiven are to forgive, giving up the claim to repay and handing the wrong to God, who judges justly. Forgiving is often slow, especially after deep harm. It isn't forgetting or excusing. Trust needs the offender's repentance, and time to rebuild. It doesn't require a victim to return to danger, or to hide a crime from those charged with justice.

If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. The door stands open. The call is to turn.

A clear film on what Christians believe, read straight from the Bible. Where faithful Christians differ, the film names the views and takes no side.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Worship
0:10 What Christians confess
0:23 Bowing and serving
0:38 The goal of the rescue
0:54 Songs and prophets
1:15 In spirit and in truth
1:44 The first gatherings
2:13 Where Christians differ
3:00 The rest of the week

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
John 4:23: "But a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth, for the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him."
Romans 12:1: "Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
What is worship, really? The singing on a Sunday morning? A quiet prayer? A feeling? And who gets to say how it's done?

Christians confess that worship is the whole response of God's people to who God is and what He has done. It's owed to the true God alone. And it can't be pulled apart from how we treat our neighbor.

The Bible's words are concrete. The most common Hebrew word means to bow down. Another means to serve. It names Israel's hard service to Pharaoh. It also names the service the LORD called Israel out of Egypt to give Him.

So the exodus is a move from one service to another. God tells Moses the sign will be that they worship Him on this mountain. Then comes the golden calf, and Aaron proclaims a feast to the LORD. The people tried to worship the LORD in a form He had forbidden.

The Psalms gave Israel words for praise and thanks, confession and lament. But the prophets judged worship by obedience. Through Amos, the LORD says He hates the feasts of a people who deny justice. Micah sums up what the LORD requires. To act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God.

People fell down and worshiped Jesus. He accepted it, though He insisted worship belongs to God alone. A Samaritan woman asked Him where worship belongs, on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem. Jesus replied. But a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth, for the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him. The place of worship is no longer a mountain. It's a person.

The first Christians met in the temple courts and in homes, for teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer. Around 112, a Roman governor named Pliny reported that they met before dawn and sang a hymn to Christ as to a god. Around 155, Justin Martyr described a Sunday in Rome. The apostles and prophets were read, bread and wine were blessed, and a collection was taken for widows, orphans and the needy.

Christians differ over how to order worship. Presbyterian and Reformed churches hold the regulative principle. In public worship, the church does only what God commands in Scripture. Lutheran, Anglican and many other Protestants hold the normative principle. The church may use what Scripture doesn't forbid, if it agrees with the gospel and builds up the church. Orthodox, Catholic and many Anglican and Lutheran Christians see their worship as sharing in heaven's worship, centered on the Eucharist and ordered by an ancient liturgy. Many Baptist, free-church, Pentecostal and charismatic Christians prefer simple forms and freedom for the Spirit to lead, with everything done in order. Every tradition has found that how a church worships shapes what it believes.

Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time. So sacrifice now describes the whole of life. Sunday's gathering trains the heart for the rest of the week. Work done honestly. Money shared. Enemies forgiven. The kitchen, the office and the hospital room are places of service to God, as truly as the sanctuary. And worship shapes the worshiper. What a person praises, fears and loves most will shape who they become.

Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship. Worship begins with God's worth, not our mood. And the Bible ends in a city where His servants will worship Him.

hist-the-apostolic-age.description:
The story of the church, told in an animated film: what happened, why it mattered, and where Christians read it differently.

Watch, read every word, and study further: https://www.livewellbyjamesbell.co/theology/history/the-apostolic-age

CHAPTERS
0:00 The first Christians
0:19 Along Roman roads
0:39 Scattered
1:03 Rome
1:28 After the apostles
1:44 Three pastors
2:16 One body
2:39 What held them
3:09 Read in different ways

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Acts 8:4: "Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
How did a few dozen frightened people in one borrowed room in Jerusalem become a church across the Roman world? They followed a teacher Rome had executed as a criminal. They had no army, no money and no protection. They should have vanished inside a generation.

They didn't. The message went on foot and by ship along Roman roads, and within a single lifetime there were assemblies in Antioch, Corinth, Ephesus and Rome. No central office directed it. The believers spoke instead of a Spirit poured out at Pentecost, and a tomb they insisted was empty.

The first believers were Jews, and the first conflict was a family quarrel among Jews over whether the crucified Jesus was the promised Messiah. Stephen was stoned, and the church in Jerusalem was scattered. Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went. And Saul of Tarsus, who had hunted believers, became the apostle Paul, founding their assemblies for the rest of his life.

Then Rome noticed. In 64, the emperor Nero blamed Christians for the fire that burned much of the city. Peter and Paul are both remembered as dying there in those years. The believers didn't fight back. But they refused what the empire demanded, a pinch of incense to Caesar as lord. They had only one Lord. And some who watched them die so calmly came in.

Then the apostles died. What happens to a movement when the eyewitnesses are gone? The answer came through leaders we call the Apostolic Fathers, who had known the apostles or their students. Their letters are the earliest Christian writings we have outside the New Testament.

Around the year 96, Clement of Rome wrote to the quarreling church at Corinth, pleading for order and humility. Around 110, Ignatius of Antioch wrote letters from the road to his death in Rome, urging the churches to stay united around their bishop. Polycarp of Smyrna, who had known the apostle John, was put to death as an old man, refusing to curse the Christ he had served for eighty-six years. These were pastors under fire, writing to keep their people faithful and together.

Their churches sat hundreds of miles apart. News moved at the speed of a walking man or a sailing ship. Yet they acted like one body. They carried letters, tested traveling teachers, and sent money to churches in famine. Churches Ignatius had never seen sent delegates to meet him. It wasn't perfect. But the pull toward one body was strong.

So what held them? Not the New Testament as one book. Settling which writings belonged took most of two centuries. Four things held them instead. A rule of faith, a short summary of the story passed down by word of mouth. Worship, the baptism and the breaking of bread that bound a believer in Rome to a believer in Antioch. A line of trusted leaders, who had learned from those who had learned from the apostles. And the Spirit they believed lived among them.

Christians read that line of leaders differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians see in it the line of bishops that has guarded the faith ever since. Many Protestants see faithful witnesses, whose words are weighed by Scripture. Both start from the same letters. This film doesn't choose between them.

We hold the finished Scripture, and it's easy to think the first believers had less than we do. They had less paper. They didn't have less faith. They held to a crucified and risen Lord, and they held to one another. We came in late. We could learn from how they waited.

The story of the church, told in an animated film: what happened, why it mattered, and where Christians read it differently.

Watch, read every word, and study further: https://www.livewellbyjamesbell.co/theology/history/the-age-of-martyrs

CHAPTERS
0:00 The age of the martyrs
0:16 What Rome wanted
0:41 A pinch of incense
0:58 The witnesses
1:19 Perpetua and Felicity
1:50 The storms
2:35 The ones who failed
3:09 A company of the forgiven
3:23 The seed

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
Mark 14:50: "Then everyone deserted Him and fled."
John 21:13: "Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Many picture the early church under Rome as one long manhunt, legions combing the provinces for believers. That picture is wrong. The real question is harder. Why would anyone die rather than say one word?

From Nero in 64 until 313, persecution was mostly local and occasional, the work of mobs and governors. Around 112 a governor named Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan. Trajan answered, don't seek Christians out, but punish any who are accused and won't recant. So the church lived legal enough to grow, and illegal enough to die.

Rome didn't want agreement. It wanted a gesture. A pinch of incense, a word calling Caesar lord, and the accused walked free. Rome had room for one more god. It couldn't tolerate refusal, and Christians would worship Jesus and no one else.

Around 165 the philosopher Justin was put to death in Rome. Asked to sacrifice, he said no right-thinking person deserts truth for falsehood. In 177, in Lyons, a slave girl named Blandina, whom her friends thought too frail to hold out, died still confessing Christ.

In 203, in Carthage, a twenty-two-year-old mother named Perpetua was arrested with a pregnant slave, Felicity. In her prison diary, her father begs her, weeping, to think of her nursing son and say the word. She points to a water jug. Can it be called anything but what it is? Neither can she. She is a Christian. She and Felicity died together. A philosopher, a slave, a young mother, and not one would say the word.

Then plague, invasion and inflation shook the empire. Emperors looking for a cause found the people who wouldn't sacrifice. In 250 Decius ordered everyone to sacrifice and carry a certificate proving it. Many died. Many more complied. In 258 Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, was executed. He met the sentence with the words, thanks be to God. In 303 Diocletian ordered churches torn down, Scriptures burned, and at last everyone made to sacrifice. In 311 a dying Galerius granted grudging toleration. Two years later Constantine made the faith legal. Rome hadn't grown kind. It had given up.

Most Christians weren't heroes. Later the lapsed, who had given in, came back ashamed, asking to return. A Roman priest named Novatian said they could never be restored. His case was serious. The martyrs had died rather than say the word. Cyprian and the larger church chose a slower, harder way. The lapsed could return through real repentance, case by case. After all, the church's own Lord had been abandoned by every man He trained. Then everyone deserted Him and fled.

And afterward, on a beach, He fed them breakfast. Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish. The body of Christ isn't a hall of the undefeated. It's a company of the forgiven.

Around 197 Tertullian told Rome the blood of Christians is seed. True, but deaths alone argued no one into faith. Christians stayed in plague cities and nursed the dying, pagans too. They took in abandoned babies and seated slave beside senator. The church refused to make dying a strategy. Courage was demanded when the hour came, never as a performance.

Within a century, Christians held the empire's power and began to reach for the sword. The people of the catacombs became the people of the courtroom. What held the martyrs up was a settled conviction that Jesus was Lord and Caesar was not. Most of us have never been asked their question. The era asks for more than admiration. It asks whom we worship.

The story of the church, told in an animated film: what happened, why it mattered, and where Christians read it differently.

Watch, read every word, and study further: https://www.livewellbyjamesbell.co/theology/history/the-great-councils

CHAPTERS
0:00 Nicaea to Chalcedon
0:16 Why the words mattered
0:35 Alexandria
0:58 Nicaea, 325
1:29 The long fight
1:47 Constantinople, 381
2:16 Ephesus, 431
2:49 Chalcedon, 451
3:09 What it cost

SCRIPTURE IN THIS FILM
John 1:1: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
John 1:14: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us."
All Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).

FULL NARRATION
Why would Christians fight over one word? It sounds like the smallest argument there is. But underneath the great councils sat the largest question anyone can ask. Who is Jesus, and what does it mean to call Him God?

The church had worshiped Jesus from the beginning. But it had no agreed words yet for what it had always believed. The whole gospel hung on it. If Jesus isn't truly God, the cross is a noble death and nothing more. If He isn't truly human, our flesh was never touched by salvation.

The first crisis carried the name of Arius, a priest in Alexandria. He taught, with real intelligence and piety, that the Son was the highest creature, but still a creature. It sounded reverent. But a created savior can't bridge the gap between God and man. The argument split the eastern churches. Crowds chanted slogans in the streets.

In 325 the emperor Constantine, wanting unity in his empire, called bishops from across the world to Nicaea. It was the first time the scattered church had gathered like this. They settled it. The Son is of the same substance as the Father, true God from true God, begotten, not made. They borrowed a word that isn't in Scripture to protect what Scripture means. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

Nicaea didn't end the fight. For most of the next fifty-six years, emperors backed the Arian side. Athanasius of Alexandria, who defended Nicaea most stubbornly, was exiled five times. The truth didn't win because it was powerful. It won slowly, against power.

By 381 a new question had surfaced. If the Son is fully God, what about the Holy Spirit? The council at Constantinople, under the emperor Theodosius, confessed the Spirit as Lord and giver of life, worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son. Three teachers called the Cappadocians showed how the one God is one substance and three persons. Not three gods, and not one God wearing masks.

Then the church had to ask how one Christ could be both God and man at once. The councils weren't pure. Rivalry between Alexandria and Antioch and imperial politics turned theology into a contest for power. At Ephesus in 431 the dispute was whether Mary could be called the bearer of God, and so whether her child was truly God from the first moment. Nestorius, the bishop of Constantinople, was condemned, partly for what he taught and partly for the politics that crushed him.

At Chalcedon in 451 the church reached its great settlement. Jesus Christ is one person in two natures, fully God and fully man. The natures are united without confusion, never blended into some third thing, and without separation, never split into two sons.

Chalcedon itself didn't unite the church. Ancient churches in Egypt, Syria and the East did not accept it, and that break has never healed. Christians still read that council differently, and that wound is real. Yet the definitions hold. The man on the cross was God, so the love shown there is God's own. And He was truly human, so our flesh and death were carried into God. Take either away and the gospel falls apart.

The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. When you say Jesus is fully God and fully man, you stand on ground that quarreling bishops marked out under fire. We didn't earn it. The least we owe is to know what it cost, and to hold it as carefully as they did.
